                                                           Abstract
      We study efficient algorithms for recovering cliques in dense random intersection graphs (RIGs).
      In this model, d = nΩ(1) cliques of size approximately k are randomly planted by choosing the ver-
      tices to participate in each clique independently with probability δ. While there has been extensive
      work on recovering one, or multiple disjointly planted cliques in random graphs, the natural exten-
      sion of this question to recovering overlapping cliques has been, surprisingly, largely unexplored.
      Moreover, because every vertex can be part of polynomially many cliques, this task is significantly
      harder than in case of disjointly planted cliques (as recently studied by Kothari, Vempala, Wein and
      Xu [COLT’23]).
           In this work we obtain the first efficient algorithms for recovering the community structure
      of RIGs both from the perspective of exact and approximate recovery. Our algorithms are further
      robust to noise, pmonotone adversaries, a certain, optimal number of edge corruptions, and work
      whenever k ≫ n log(n). Our techniques follow the proofs-to-algorithms framework utilizing
      the sum-of-squares hierarchy. An essential component are certificates for the absence of large
      cliques outside of the ground-truth. Instead of spectral certificates, a central ingredient are mod-
      ified versions of the biclique certificates, recently used for semi-random planted clique by Buhai,
      Kothari and Steurer [STOC’23]. To turn these certificates into robust and efficient algorithms that
      do not produce “false positives”, we rely on an extremely sharp concentration property for pseudo-
      distributions which might be of independent interest.
           Our techniques further extend to the related task of efficient refutation, and lead to algorithms
      that can not only recover the ground-truth, but also certify the optimality of this clustering.1
      Keywords: Sum of Squares, Robust Algorithms, Community Detection, Random Intersection
      Graphs

computer science and machine learning. It was one of the first problems shown to be NP-complete

containing cliques of size n1−ε (Høastad, 1999; Zuckerman, 2006), which has led to the emergence

and it initiated the search for new algorithms that remain robust in semirandom settings as described
above, see (Feige and Krauthgamer, 2000b; Moitra et al., 2016; Buhai et al., 2023) for examples.
Moitra et al. (2016), have even shown that a monotone adversary can shift the information-theoretic
threshold for weak recovery in the stochastic block model, thereby rendering the problem strictly
harder even though it only makes “helpful” changes.
Prior Work From an algorithmic viewpoint, our setting was previously studied by Nikoletseas
et al. (2021) who gave a simple inefficient algorithm for recovering the community structure of a
dense RIG, thus showing that exact recovery is information-theoretically feasible. Subsequently,
Christodoulou et al. (2023) experimentally studied a spectral heuristic for this problem, but they
were not able to give provable performance guarantees. Surprisingly, our results in Section 2.2
show that this approach provably does not work, at least if d is sufficiently large. In (Nikoletseas
et al., 2021) and (Christodoulou et al., 2023), finding an efficient algorithm for exact recovery with
provable performance guarantees was therefore left as an open problem. It was further suggested as
a future direction in (Bresler et al., 2025, Section 3, (2)). In the sufficiently sparse regime (where
p = n−c for sufficiently large exponent c), some simple efficient combinatorial algorithms are
known (Behrisch et al., 2009; Behrisch and Taraz, 2006). However, all these approaches break in
the dense case.

Related Work With regard to community detection, it is further important to point out that RIGs
have some resemblance with mixed membership stochastic block models (MMSBs) which have been
studied as a model for overlapping community detection before, see (Hopkins and Steurer, 2017;
Anandkumar et al., 2013). We discuss the similarities and differences between these two models in
more detail in Appendix A.3. For now, we emphasize that the main differences between community
detection in MMSBs and our setting are that (i) we achieve stronger recovery guarantees as previous
work (exact/approximate recovery for every community instead of weak recovery in (Anandkumar
et al., 2013; Hopkins and Steurer, 2017)), (ii) we focus on the high-dimensional setting where the
number of communities grows polynomially in n, and (iii) we put emphasis on the robustness of our
algorithms, while the known algorithms for MMSBs cannot handle (even monotone) adversaries.

2. Techniques
Our algorithms are an instantiation of the so-called proofs-to-algorithms framework (for an excellent
exposition see for example (Fleming et al., 2019)) that utilizes the sum-of-squares hierarchy. The
general idea is that an algorithm follows from two ingredients. First, a mechanism for certifying
“goodness” of a solution candidate, and second, a proof of identifiability which states that any
solution that passes our certification step is close to the underlying ground-truth set of parameters
we are trying to estimate.

2.1. Simple, inefficient algorithm
Our approach towards a simple, correct (yet inefficient) algorithm follows a similar high-level idea
as employed in previous work for average-case clustering problems (see for example (Bakshi et al.,
2020; Fleming et al., 2019)). Specifically, we enumerate over all possible clusters (in our case
subsets of roughly k vertices) and check if they “seem like one of the clusters we are looking for”.

2.2. Towards efficient and robust algorithms
Hence, to obtain an efficient, robust algorithm, the main challenge in making the above ideas work
is to find new ways of “certifying” that any sufficiently large clique in G has large overlap with
some set Sℓ . This will be the main focus for the rest of this section.

A.1. Parameter assumptions
An important assumption with regard to the parameters in all G ∼ RIG(n, d, p, q) we consider is
that d ⩾ nα for some (arbitrarily small) constant α > 0, and that p is bounded away from 1, i.e.,
that there is some (arbitrarily small) ε > 0 such that p ⩽ 1 − ε. Constants hidden in Landau-
notation typically depend linearly on α and ε and generally get worse as α, ε → 0. With regard to
the assumption p ⩽ 1 − ε, this is at many places necessary as distinguishing a clique from the rest
of the graph generally becomes harder the denser the overall graph becomes. On the other hand,
we generally believe that the assumption α > 0 is not necessary, as our problem should generally

other variants of planted clique as well, see e.g. Kothari et al. (2023a); Barak et al. (2019)).

the other hand, for small d, the number of planted cliques is quite small and k is quite large, which
simplifies other steps. While we believe an extension of our analysis to the case of any d or at least
sufficiently large d to be possible, we do not expect this to yield significant new insights.

A.2. From dense to sparse graphs
Throughout the rest of this paper, we generally make the assumption that the overall edge-density
p is a constant, while both our algorithms and Theorem 7 continue to hold if p = o(1) as well.
The reason we can still assume p = Ω(1) is that these dense graphs form the hard instances for our
problem, and everything we do in the dense regime actually carries over directly to the sparse case.
    Concretely, we achieve this because our algorithms are robust to a monotone adversary, and
since we have a simple coupling argument showing that any RIG with small p can be transformed
into an RIG with p = 1/2 (or any other constant) simply by “ramping up” the noise levels given
by q while all ground-truth cliques are kept intact. Our algorithms and theorems then apply to this
“densified” graph, which can be turned back into the original one using a monotone adversary. This
is why it is not a restriction to assume p ⩾ 1/2 throughout the rest of this work. Our coupling is
formally captured in the following lemma, which is proved in Appendix J.

Lemma 10 Consider G ∼ RIG(n, d, p, q) with nα ≪ d ≪ n2−α for some arbitrarily small α > 0
and arbitrary p, q, q < p. Then, for every 12 ⩾ p′ > p, there exists some q ′ > q such that G can
be coupled to G′ ∼ RIG(n, d, p′ , q ′ ). such that G ⊆ G′ while for every ℓ ∈ [d], the ground-truth
cliques Sℓ are identical in both G and G′ .

A.3. Comparison with Mixed Membership Stochastic Block Models (MMSBs)
In this section, we provide a comparison between our model and algorithms to the results obtained
in previous work on overlapping community detection.
    Detecting overlapping communities has received less attention (at least from a rigorous math-
ematical standpoint), however, most existing work has focused on so called mixed membership
stochastic block models (MMSBs) that share some similarities with RIGs (see e.g. Coja-Oghlan
(2010); Krzakala et al. (2013); Anandkumar et al. (2013); Bordenave et al. (2015); Abbe and San-
don (2015); Mossel et al. (2015); Guédon and Vershynin (2016); Montanari and Sen (2016); Yun
and Proutiere (2016); Hopkins and Steurer (2017); Amini and Levina (2018); Mao et al. (2021) but
also the survey by Abbe Abbe (2017) and references therein). The purpose of this section is to
discuss the similarities and differences of these models and to contrast the algorithmic guarantees
considered in this and previous works. We start with the definition of MMSBs.

Definition 11 We define MMSB(n, s, ε, d, β) as the distribution over graphs on vertex set n ob-
tained using the following procedure.

Here, the vectors σv represent the fractional community memberships of v. The probability that
two vertices u, v are adjacent is larger if the two vectors σi , σj share similar features. In total, this
gives rise to d communities where community ℓ ∈ [d] is defined by all vertices v for which σv (ℓ)
is “large”. The parameter β controls the amount of overlap between communities. Specifically, in

communities like in the classical stochastic block model. On the other hand, for non-zero β the
“large” values of σv concentrate on roughly β uniformly random coordinates of each σv . This has
the intuitive interpretation that each vertex is a member of approximately β communities.
Stronger notions of recovery RIGs are conceptually similar if we think of {0, 1}d -valued com-
munity membership vectors σv that arise as the characteristic vectors of the sets Mv . Two vertices
are then adjacent if and only if ⟨σu , σv ⟩ ̸= 0 (in the noiseless case). Hence, the main difference
between RIGs and MMSBs is that RIGs do not allow for fractional community memberships. This
allows a much less ambiguous and combinatorial definition of which vertices participate in a given
community and thus enables us to study stronger notions of recovery (formalized in Theorem 2):
we require our algorithms to find exactly d communities such that for every ground-truth commu-
nity K we recover almost all vertices that participate in K. This is a key difference to previous
work Anandkumar et al. (2013); Hopkins and Steurer (2017), where the goal is weak recovery that
merely requires finding a community assignment which is non-trivially correlated with the ground-
truth. Here, a community assignment can have high correlation with the ground-truth even if entire
communities are completely “ignored”. This is especially true if the number of communities tends
to infinity with n. Our algorithms achieve performance guarantees that explicitly exclude such
outcomes.
Limitations of tensor-based approaches in RIGs Another important difference between MMSBs
and RIGs is that RIGs do not make a distinction between edges that appear in only one community
versus edges that appear in two or more communities. Specifically, if we consider a set of vertices
S, then in a MMSB, the graph induced by S will become denser the more shared communities the
vertices in S participate in. In RIGs on the other hand, there is no distinction between the vertices
in S having one versus many communities in common. Mathematically, this amounts to a certain
“non-linearity” when estimating moments of the hidden variables given the posterior (i.e. the graph
arising from them).

B.3. When do balanced subgraphs appear?
After having proved Lemma 19, it remains to give a criterion for when balanced subgraphs actually
appear in a G ∼ RIG(n, d, p, q). We        formalize this in Lemma 21 which on a high level states
the following. If we fix a T ∈ [n]      t   and use a procedure that constructs a bipartite sub-graph

C.3. SoS Certificates in balanced bipartite graphs
The core of the analysis of all our algorithms is an SoS-certificate for the absence of bicliques in
balanced bipartite graphs. Before formally describing our certificates, we introduce some notation.
Recall that given a bipartite graph G = A ⊎ B, we denote variables for vertices v ∈ A by xv and
variables for vertices v ∈ B by yv . We further denote by x ∈ R|A| the vector of all variables xv for
v ∈ A and by y ∈ R|B| the vector of all variables yv for v ∈ B. Given a vector x of variables,
                                                                                         Q        we
denote by |x| its L1 -norm. Moreover, for a set S ⊆ [n], we use the abbreviation xS := i∈S xi .

With this, we introduce the main lemma upon which our biclique certificates are built. It can be

D.3. Algorithmic Refutation
In addition to the fact that the ideas from Lemma D.2 yield a better single label clique theorem,
they have algorithmic consequences. Since everything can be stated in terms of low-degree SoS, a
certificate that no cliques outside of the ground-trugh exist can actually be computed in polynomial
time.
    This has a curious consequence in light of our algorithm for exact recovery from Theorem 3:
after termination, the algorithm can actually certify that it is correct in the sense that it outputs a list
L of cliques and a certificate proving that no other clique of size (1 − ε)k exists that is not contained
in one of the cliques in L. Moreover, if we simply want a certificate that no clique of a certain size
(1 + ε)k exists without prior knowledge of the ground truth cliques, this can also be computed in
polynomial time. We capture these two facts in the following theorem.

Here, edges within some ground truth community form with probability q ↑ while edges outside
form with probability q ↓< q ↑. Can our algorithms be extended to this case? The techniques
presented in Appendix F partially cover the case where up to a constant fraction of edges (that are
adversarially chosen) are missing in the ground-truth Sℓ , but they do not directly extend to the two-
sided case. Here, a significantly larger number of missing edges has to be handled, which, however,
is not adversarially chosen but random. We believe our techniques to be a good starting point for
achieving recovery in RIG2 (n, d, p, q ↑, q ↓), but some further ideas will be required. Moreover,
it would be interesting to see if the algorithms on RIGs with two-sided noise can still be made
robust to a monotone adversary that is now not only allowed to delete edges outside of the ground-
truth communities, but also to add back edges within the communities. We believe this to be the
case, however it is known that the capabilities of a such adversary do shift the information-theoretic
threshold for recoverability in the stochastic block model Moitra et al. (2016), so this question stil
deserves a formal investigation.

Hardness of recovery in dense RIGs without noise Moreover, it would be very interesting to
better understand the computational-statistical trade-offs for recovering communities in RIGs. We
                                                                     √
show in Appendix I that recovery is hard in the noisy model if k ≪ n like it is the case for classi-
cal planted clique. Together with the information-theoretic feasibility proved in Appendix D.1, this
                                                                            √
shows that there is a computational-statistical gap whenever nε ≪ k ≪ n and p, q are a suffi-
ciently small constants. However, our reduction from planted clique in Theorem 87 crucially relies
on the fact that we have independent edges outside of the communities in our model RIG(n, d, p, q).
     It would be very interesting to find out if this hardness carries over to the case where p is
a constant and q = 0, i.e., the dense, noiseless case. We strongly believe this to be the case,
however, finding evidence for a such computational statistical gap seems to be quite challenging.
While there are multiple ways of giving evidence for such gaps exist (e.g. low-degree polynomials,
SoS lower bounds, the overlap gap property, statistical query algorithms, reductions from other
statistical problems), none of the techniques known to us seems to easily handle dense, noiseless
RIGs. Finding such techniques would likely be interesting in its own right and might further shed
light on other computational aspects of other average-case problems.
